beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new, it's just the module title

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing the agent isn't the thing; context, a skill, output or an interface is, and the real problem is whether people take it up.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: nothing new, though I have Confluence AI search that nobody uses

beats.trigger: **Name** the likely adoption failure before it happens, including the social failure that's hardest to see
beats.got: The outcomes list is long and mostly consulting vocabulary. Only the failure-naming bullet interests me.

beats.trigger: And what makes you hesitate about actually handing this to them?
beats.got: I do hesitate, because I'd be the one stuck maintaining it.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: JTBD framing: start from the teammate's job, not from my tool. Fair, but I know it already.

beats.trigger: If it could describe anyone in the room, point to the generic line and ask the agent to try that part again.
beats.got: The agent interviews me and I check whether the jtbd file is specific. It's a decent check, but it feels like ceremony.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is a vendor pitch and is NOT on the list.
beats.got: There are four sharing shapes, and the whole-agent option is deliberately excluded. That gives me a vocabulary for what I'd build for sales.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a handoff to the next exercise

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new, just setup for the next two steps

beats.trigger: The obstacle is usually not the first technical limitation a builder sees.
beats.got: The real blocker is usually social, political or trust-related, not technical. Looking for the load-bearing obstacle is a useful move.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: My plans would look exactly like that: a great technical file and a people file full of UNASSIGNED.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a handoff

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are hypotheses, not a rollout. I'd already assumed that.

beats.trigger: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: The question is why someone would drop what they use today for mine. I haven't asked that about my sales setup.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem with three failure stories, and the strongest one becomes a single conversation. This is the useful kind of failure-mode work.

beats.trigger: Test the switch, not the solution.
beats.got: A four-line recap of what I just did

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new, just the lecture intro

beats.trigger: A good interview finds a third outcome past speed and quality: a dependency removed, an anxiety gone, a scope widened.
beats.got: Beyond speed and quality, a good outcome can also be removing a dependency or an anxiety. That's a slightly new angle.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and they run it, get a generic answer, and quietly stop.
beats.got: The agent file is just instructions, and the value sits in the memory and corrections around it. I've seen exactly that happen when I shared a repo.

beats.trigger: An agent is context, a boundary, a set of checks and somebody who answers for what it does.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy in an afternoon, but the person who answers for it doesn't. For my sales setup that person is me by default.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: Rollout dashboards count access as if it were adoption, and mine do too.

beats.trigger: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: People take up things that resemble their own work. A bit philosophical for me, but fine.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: Interfaces depend on someone else's calendar, unlike the earlier modules' pieces.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: A multi-agent org redesign with 15 people was done well and then died because leadership's urgency moved on. That's a failure mode I hadn't met.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: The answers to the switch question are small and specific, like landing where they already look and having a trusted person go first. Peers matter more than the pitch.

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: nothing new, uptake is their call

beats.trigger: The technical plan fills quickly. The people plan stalls on names.
beats.got: A missing name is a finding, and the move is one person who'd tell you plainly if it didn't help.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed.
beats.got: nothing new, it's an agent review-and-rewrite step, and I'd skip it

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
beats.got: nothing new, just housekeeping

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: nothing new, a recap

beats.trigger: Test one assumption. Ask for one name. Talk to one person.
beats.got: I have to actually talk to someone before Module 8, and building something over the weekend doesn't count.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a teaser for Module 8

take_homes: Three of an agent's four parts (context, boundary, checks) copy fast, but the person who answers for it doesn't, and that person is me by default.
Before building the sales setup, find one named person in sales and ask what job they're doing today and what they use now.
Ask 'what would have to be true for them to drop what they use today?' Don't count access as adoption.

monday.move: Ask one sales ops person how they do their weekly pipeline prep today, and ask who would own a shared agent if it existed.
monday.who: One person in sales ops. I don't have the name yet and need to ask the head of sales.
monday.when: Tuesday, a 20-minute chat. Monday is for finding the name.
monday.stop_condition: They say it's not a pain, or nobody will own it.
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering asked for it. I'm tempted to build it first anyway.

misconception.why: The line about output that 'looked fine and was not' made me think my review-skipping is the very judgement my teammates wouldn't inherit. I still think checking matters less for me personally. The module is about people, not verification, so it only half-landed.

one_line: Basics were slow, but the 'you can't share an agent, only context, skills, output or an interface, and the owner doesn't copy' idea is worth it for anyone about to roll out to non-engineers.
